sources.authors: Bratthall, Figueira, Nording
sources.source_byte_caveat: PMC peer-reviewed original full HTML directly inspected 2026-11-09, PubMed PMID 38434259 and Umea/SciLifeLab indexed identity crosschecked; HTML/PDF binary not downloaded or SHA-256 hashed. Original figures and supplementary raw tables not reanalyzed.
sources.claims_verified_externally: Bratthall, Figueira, Nording, Heliyon 10(5) e26625 (online Feb 17 2024; collection Mar 15). Methods: one dark 100% Arabica commercial blend coarse French-press grind, 11g/200mL, 93C, five minute immersion/filter, 9 groups (pure-water control; MgCl2/CaCl2 100/1000ppm as salts either before or after brew) n=5/group. Four measured organic acids citric/malic/lactic/quinic using GC-MS and NMR; 100ppm salts produced little/no change in measured acids, most pre/post comparisons similar; at 1000ppm analytical methods diverged, with salt-induced complexation/spectral effects possible. Bicarbonate/normal mixed water ions excluded. No espresso brewing, five-taste sensory experiment, subjective acidity perception or measured espresso recipe outcome. Cannot treat ppm of chloride SALT as ppm of elemental magnesium/calcium, assert water-independent flavor or universal mineral dose.

sources.claims_verified_externally: Original author's homogeneous-flow mathematical model predicts greater EY with finer grind, while the cafe experiment under 6 bar (lowered from 9 bar because of fine-grind clogging) observes a peaked EY-versus-grind relationship with lower EY/greater variation at very fine settings. A 20g-to-15g dose reduction/coarser-grind cafe protocol, shorter ~14s shots and sales-based coffee-cost case illustrate operational efficiency, NOT randomized preferred espresso flavor or personal five-input DIC outcomes. EY/TDS, time, taste and economic success are different measured outcomes, and neither fine-grind 'critical point' nor a brew-time target transfers universally across grinders, burrs, coffees, feeds, pressure and baskets.

sources.source_byte_caveat: 6-page author arXiv:2206.12373v2 original text and selected PDF page images directly examined; full PDF bytes not separately saved/hashed, publisher 7-page final version and university accepted-manuscript PDF unavailable; no independent reproduction, raw measurements or supplements.
sources.claims_verified_externally: R455-246 university DOI/author publication identity + full author arXiv v2 Table I/figures/discussion. Experimental points are earlier Cameron 2020 data, whereas Lee adds a fitted two-equal-pathway model. Empirical coffee density 399 kg/m3 versus explicitly imposed unphysical 798 kg/m3 is necessary for the model to produce the declining fine-grind extraction limb; with physical value model flattens. Three averaged composite chemistries cannot establish causal chemistry-to-preference correlations. No external funding stated; Kamira manufacturer supplied the device and technical guidance; author Nicola Cicero reports Science4life consultancy. Original raw results available on request, not obtained.

sources.authors: Mackenzie E. Batali; Lik Xian Lim; Jiexin Liang; Sara E. Yeager; Ashley N. Thompson; Juliet Han; William D. Ristenpart; Jean-Xavier Guinard

sources.claims_verified_externally: Original Methods §§2.1-2.6: 27 3x3x3 factorial samples (one Ethiopian washed, one El Salvador honey, one Sumatra wet-hulled coffee, each light/medium/dark, immersion at 4/22/92 C) prepared in triplicate. All 27 brewed to extraction equilibrium for hours, had different starting extraction percentages, then diluted to exactly 2% TDS and uniformly chilled and served at 4 C. COVID home descriptive panel training began with 20, 17 entered formal evaluation, 14 completed and four excluded for inconsistent replicate scoring, leaving 10 retained panelists. Scores were 0-100 for 27 trained terms, not five DIC sliders. Across tested roasts/origins, authors report hot immersion samples more bitter, sour and rubbery, cold more floral, with roast/origin interaction. Temperature altered pH more consistently than titratable acidity, which did not systematically change with brewing temperature. Discussion explicitly notes no compound-level chemistry, residual percentage-extraction differences, long hot-steeping aroma loss and uncontrolled consumption lighting. Funded by Coffee Science Foundation underwritten by Toddy LLC cold brewing equipment supplier; no conflicts declared.

sources.title: Chemical characterization and sensory evaluation of a phenolic-rich melanoidin isolate contributing to coffee astringency
sources.authors: Brianne M. Linne; Edisson Tello; Christopher T. Simons; Devin G. Peterson
sources.access: DIRECT_PRIMARY_PUBLISHER_FULL_HTML_METHODS_SENSORY_RESULTS_RECOMBINATION_DISCUSSION_CONCLUSIONS_READ_20261111; publisher landing and PubMed cross-check; supplementary PDF and raw panel files not downloaded or independently hashed
sources.source_byte_caveat: HTML publisher full text directly reviewed; exact HTML/PDF byte digest, supplementary tables, figure pixels and independent sensory replication not verified
sources.source_details: Two preportioned commercial drip coffees described as high/low body by four Q-graders; Keurig K475 brew; sensory-guided fractionation four-person panel for UF/SPE (duplicate), five trained panelists for LC fractions (duplicate), nine trained panelists for coffee/water recombination (three evaluations each, not 27 independent people). F9.6.4 was a chemically complex phenolic/melanoidin-associated isolate, not identified as a single causal molecule. Coffee recombination from 7.8 to 15.7 mg/L gave discriminability R-index 69.5% against lower-body coffee control (reported p <= 0.01), with drying/astringent descriptions; 27 evaluations per condition reflect repeated assessments of nine people. Sensory reference and test conditions were intentionally controlled; result is not automatically transferable to espresso extraction or private 1-to-5 ratings.
sources.science_limits: No espresso comparison, no dose/grind/feed/temperature intervention, no same-coffee longitudinal sensory ratings, no machine- or roast-specific threshold, and no personal preference or universal drinkability finding. Detecting an added isolate does not prove that an astringent espresso is overextracted or justify an automatic grind/yield correction.
sources.relevance: DIC's independent Astringency / Dryness input is semantically compatible with oral roughness/drying/puckering; currently captured by site/lib/constants.js and site/lib/ui.js. sources.authors: Mathilde C. Charles; Andrea Romano; Sine Yener; Massimo Barnaba; Luciano Navarini; Tilmann D. Mark; Franco Biasioli; Flavia Gasperi
sources.source_byte_caveat: Direct text extracted from institution-hosted 2016 doctoral thesis published-article reprint; screenshot requests failed cached-PDF retrieval, so images/tables/figures NOT visually verified in this run. Original journal PDF restricted, and institution thesis PDF bytes SHA-256, individual participant raw TDS/nosespace trace data, source cross-laboratory replication and personal espresso tasting improvement not obtained.
sources.claims_verified_externally: Original article methods reproduced in coauthor doctoral thesis Chapter 4.1 §§4.1.2–4.1.5: two commercially low-caffeine Illy 100% Arabica Iperespresso capsule roast types (light A/dark B) crossed with 0 vs 100mg/mL added sucrose; espresso X7.1 prepared ~30mL but panel tasted 10mL crema-free aliquots at 55C through lidded straw. Eighteen Fondazione Edmund Mach employee volunteers ages 23–37 (only THREE with prior sensory work), trained over approximately two months; four samples three repeats per person, balancing sessions, nine temporal dominant descriptors; NOT DIC five independent 1–5 member-intensity sliders. Concurrent in-vivo PTR-ToF-MS nosespace; original data reduction retained 39 peaks × six temporal measures =234 columns × 72 subject-condition aggregates. Added sucrose substantially shifted perceived dominance toward sweet/caramel/nutty and masked sour/bitter, with little measured nosespace aroma-release change; darker roasting showed more volatile signal and altered bitter/burnt/roasted dominance. These are experimental condition associations, not a calibrated app sweetness recommendation or trial of changing espresso shot recipe, and do not establish a universal flavor score or objective personal espresso success.
sources.locked_policy_boundary: Maintain the five independently completed DIC taste ratings, valid all-green vs missing distinction and ONE genuinely controllable next-shot action; no external sweetness chemistry inference or sugar input; preserve original dose/yield/time, private notes/history and multiple successful recipe families, independent Turbo/Fast-Flow/Slow Feed, grinder calibration and existing equipment-specific temperature. Same burr setting showed both treated beans flowed faster than control; second comparison adjusted grinders separately to approximately 1mL/s, giving Warm 0.97+/-0.07 and Cold 1.06+/-0.08 mL/s. Triplicate independent experiments with five measurement replicates. Thermal treatments had altered PSD, lowered caffeine concentration versus control, cooling reduced CGAs versus control, warm had more hexanal; TDS not statistically different among flow-matched sets. Experiments did not isolate thermal-vs-oxidative exposure, prove slower everyday bean prefeed or human taste benefit. The paper's sentence attributing increased flow to decreased permeability appears physically inconsistent and is not accepted as an established causal direction.
sources.locked_policy_boundary: No pregrind oven/chiller or dosing prescription, universal temperature or caffeine reduction advice, grinder setting translation, measured shot rewriting, non-sensory taste score or new feed-mode correction. evidence_checks.claim: The original article compares two coffees (Square Mile Tumba Rwanda and Guayacán Colombia), each at 11 grind settings: 22 physical XCT-based ground-coffee packs. evidence_checks.claim: Study-specific TEP barista/panel brewing standard gives 15-17g basket dose, 70-90mL double serving (volume, not measured grams), 25 +/-3s, 92-94C and 9 bar; Table 3 specifies study water. Table 2's printed 'Extraction Ratio 50-55% coffee weight to extraction time' is dimensionally ambiguous and NOT a verified dose:beverage-mass ratio; it cannot define a DIC numeric target. Table 4 uses CATA descriptors, 0-100 overall quality, yes/no willingness, and text items, NOT DIC's five independent 1-5 tastes.

evidence_checks.source_provenance: https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/14/4/593 original publisher first-party full HTML numeric table cells; 2026-11-15
evidence_checks.page_section: Results 3.1-3.2, Tables 7/9 exact numeric cells
evidence_checks.claim: Table 7 global homogeneity index 0.364 over 138 repeated evaluations from 46 experts, with 91.3% of experts grouped with themselves by CLUSCATA; this is within-rater CATA cluster repeatability, not 91.3% predictive accuracy. Country values include Italy 71.4%, Korea 100%, USA 90%. Table 9 within-USA eight-coffee quality comparison p=0.8634, while France, India, Italy, Korea p<0.0001; expert response repeatability can coexist with no significant sample discrimination. Neither result measures member single-change next-shot taste improvement.

evidence_checks.source_provenance: Wiley original full published HTML 2026-11-15 https://ift.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1750-3841.71434
evidence_checks.page_section: Methods 2.1-2.3, Table 3
evidence_checks.claim: Same-batch medium-roast Colombian Kachalu was French-pressed, 50g grounds/900+/-5g water at ~92C for 4min; 31 and 25 untrained people in two duo-trio sessions performed 25 distinct water comparisons, not one 56-person universal espresso rating experiment. Individual Mg-only tests were non-significant; bicarbonate-only 120mg/L 20/30 correct p=.049 and 240mg/L 24/30 p<.001; Ca-only 15mg/L p=.022 isolated among nonmonotonic Ca comparisons. Discrimination is not preference or a causal five-taste recipe prescription.

evidence_checks.source_provenance: Wiley original full published HTML 2026-11-15 https://ift.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1750-3841.71434
evidence_checks.page_section: Methods 2.3.2, Results 3.2/3.3, Tables 4-5
evidence_checks.claim: Both descriptive analyses used ten trained sensory assessors with randomized triplicates and 15cm unstructured intensity scales, not the five personal 1-5 DIC ratings. DA1 all eight water-composition attribute comparisons non-significant (Table4 all p>=.276). DA2 among extreme samples showed reference vs 300mg/L bicarbonate target acidity 12.0 vs 2.9cm and fruitiness 10.2 vs 2.4cm, while astringency overall p=.485 (non-significant). Table5 ratings reflect one particular extreme French-press water contrast and cannot validate an espresso quality optimum or personal next-shot success.

evidence_checks.source_provenance: Wiley original full published HTML 2026-11-15 https://ift.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1750-3841.71434
evidence_checks.page_section: Results 3.3.2 Table 6 measured titrated bicarbonate / water and brewed coffee pH
evidence_checks.claim: Two sample waters B and C both targeted nominal 300mg/L bicarbonate, yet Table6 titrated actual concentrations were 253 vs 162mg/L, and brewed coffee pH 5.19 vs 4.88 respectively. Original authors infer CaCO3 precipitation as plausible mediator; nominal salt addition is not equivalent to actual dissolved bicarbonate. A future voluntary one-change comparison would need consistent actual water composition and plausible confounder assessment, not add water telemetry or auto-correct DIC tastes now.
